Ahead of PCE next week, a reminder to keep an eye on the breadth of price increases.

At Jackson Hole in August, Chair Kevin Warsh said that “over the past 12 months, 54% of goods and services in the PCE basket showed price increases above 3%. This is well below the post-pandemic highs of about 77%, but it remains well above the level of 32% in the two decades that preceded the pandemic.”

Running the same exercise on the CPI across the roughly 180 item categories the BLS publishes, covering about 98% of the basket, yields mixed results.

While 47.2% of categories rose more than 3% from a year earlier in September, the lowest since December and down from 50.6% in August, that compares with an average of 31.7% from 2000 to 2019 although well off the peak of 80.4% in March 2022.

And weighted by share of spending, 62.2% of the basket is rising faster than 3%, the most since September 2025, up from 60.0% in August, as the categories that crossed above 3% included larger ones such as college tuition (+4.00%), hotels (+4.27%), cable, satellite and streaming TV (+3.33%) and motor vehicle repair (+3.55%), while eight of the 17 that fell back below 3% were grocery items.

The share above 5% rose to 23.0% of categories (13.1% of the basket) from 21.0% (11.6%), led by gasoline (+34.17%), hospital services (+5.63%), dental services (+6.02%) and airline fares (+22.45%), while 27.5% of categories are now falling from a year earlier, up from 21.0%.

I guess what I've seen from Chinese laser capacity expansion: 

1. Dongshan/Source Photonics (索尔思): 9M/month capacity -> 22M/month Q4 ->  300m/year in 2027 (mostly EML, but blended)

Claims of 1B/year "target" for laser chips with no deadline, but I'd take this as a grain of salt. 

2. Shijia (仕佳): 72M/year for 100mW CW, 2-3 year project (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

3. Yunling (云岭): 18.75M/year 70/100mW CW, 3 year schedule (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

4. Ligent (纳真), some reports stated 170M target for total capacity (also blended, lot of which is 200G EML)

5. Yuanjie: ~10M/year currently, expanding for early 2027 and 2028, but no quantities. 

6. Hongchen: I think this was the perfect example of flooding H2 2026 arguments. With some some optical bears claiming 60-70M capacity...

But this turned out to completely wrong... Their actual statements were "70/100 mW products are entering small-volume production". 

7. Dingxin Optoelectronics - Targeting 15M/year blended (with 70/100mW CW and 100G EML lines)

Obviously mapped many others like Everbright/Accelink and did some guesses around laser mixes, but only included public disclosures. 

From your pluggable vendor channel checks: 

- 70mW/100mW lasers are actually a bottleneck right now per Innolight/Cambridge channel checks, laser ASPs actually increasing. 

Lasers are tighter than they were a few months ago. 

I don't think there's a giant moat here, Chinese players are already competitive. But a bottleneck is a bottleneck, and anyone with capacity to monetize that will benefit, since it's a volume game. 

In terms of what the larger pluggable makers are actually doing: 

- Innolight September disclosure: actively introducing new suppliers and are planning to sign 2-3 year-long contracts to lock upstream capacity for lasers (still actively securing supply for 1.6T pluggables)

So there's some game theory over who can lock up qualified capacity among all your players. 

Even if there's some over-ordering, laser BOM is cheap, so they'd probably want to lock up capacity with more suppliers than lose billions in downstream revenue. (also kinda hurts competitors) 

- High end lines (for CPO), non-competitive with Western players like $LITE / $COHR as of next few years. But Chinese players would eventually develop the technology. 

- $AAOI CEO: Chinese suppliers several years behind on high-power CPO/DWDM laser production "not in the next 2,3 years"

- $LITE CEO questioned whether claimed Chinese manufacturing capacity was translating into commercial output. "At least at the moment, we see no impact from any Chinese laser supply."

This is despite Shijia, Everbright, Yuanjie and others stating 400mW capabilities and capacity expansion targets from Chinese companies. Although Western CEOs might be disputing their reliability and capability to scale these lines. 

I see lower end range bottleneck for pluggable will gradually ease as more capacity comes online 2028. But all evidence points against near-term overflooding. 

The 100mW range for example, someone cited 2 years of equipment investment. Higher ranges were 3 years for equipment investment? So even some Chinese players take years for capacity to come online. 

The multi year laser shortage statements from laser company executives seems to be true... especially among higher end ranges, since buildout takes a lot of time. 

Legitimate competition coming from China, but as of now there's a scramble for CW LTAs among the industry in 2026-2027. 

Lot of capacity is probably allocated toward higher spec lasers or EML, as seen with EML bottlenecking $LITE for the longest time (they have more supply now) that they had to buy CW off the market instead of supplying it themselves. 

This is while tail end for 800G demand for example, might continue much much longer than expected with sovereign DC buildouts. So there might be some surprising dynamics for duration, we'll see.

In the end I do think supply chains will be bifurcated: 

- Chinese players will prioritize domestic capabilities but heavily sources globally. 

- Western players (now) prioritize Western supply chains unless China comes online with cheap enough supply (which don't see happening near-term). 

TLDR: 
-> Multi-year shortage definitely seems accurate for higher end specs
-> Lot of China capacity overflooding claims earlier from H1 turned out to be completely false. People keep making them for some reason across memory to photonics. 
-> Chinese laser players are competitive for 70mW/100MW, meaningful expansion Y/Y, but nothing showing overflooding, given laser demand increasing, probably gradual easing into 2028. 

We'll see, supply chain evolves month after month, just my current opinion from what I'm seeing.

Yes, I like $SIVE. It's a fun company to cover, since there's a lot of supply chain alpha here. 

But the company completely Tall Poppy Syndromed itself last earnings. 

And it's clearly shown in the drawdown. 

Bit of a longer consolidated thought and some scattered bits of supply chain info: 

- Sivers has 100M CW DFB laser capacity coming online Q4 2027 during an industry shortage. 

And very large allocations from foundries online (they were doing these quals with Win Semi + 2 others back in 2023/2024), so they can actively monetize the bottleneck today. 

The other interesting reason why bottlenecks are important (aside from ASP hikes), is because qualifications convert much faster + more likely given incentives around supply scarcity.

-> As one example, module makers have expanded the amount of suppliers, eg. (lightcounting cited companies expanding to 5-7+ suppliers from 2-3). 

Innolight, for example last month responded to a question addressing tight 1.6T DFB laser supply in 2026–2027:

- Innolight was actively introducing new suppliers last month and are planning to sign 2-3 year-long contracts to lock upstream capacity

-> This is while your biggest merchant laser companies making up the world's 600m+ EML/CW laser capacity like $COHR have redirected lasers to their own programs. $LITE sold out into 2029, Landmark also locked a lot of their capacity into 2027-2029. $AAOI was an expected player, but ended up redirecting lasers into their own transceiver programs too. 

And this coincides with times $SIVE has tremendous capacity available now + actively engaged with Chinese pluggables players (not saying it's Innolight, but just shows Chinese makers like Cambridge/Eoptolink are actively trying to secure laser capacity). 

- Fun to note, before $JBL was announced, Sivers had and has ongoing direct engagements with hyperscalers as well. 

We saw that hyperscalers approached $MTSI and $AAOI for laser capacity from their earnings transcripts (and hilariously got turned away from AAOI due to shortages).

So the odds pluggable makers or hyperscalers end up converting to capacity agreements with $SIVE seems a materially higher. 

Just a little rant: for all the sellside/retail trying to model revenue, you can't just slap on a stupid 25-35% CAGR on NRE revenue since it's close to 0 revenue now.

Especially when they scale up to maybe 300M laser capacity (extrapolated from 2:1 external/internal capacity).

It's also not the same as $POET having OE packaging capacity at scale, since lasers are in a genuine shortage. So capacity is more likely to convert like how $AAOI is sold out, $LITE is sold out into 2029  

We've already seen what revenue that laser capacity brings in since $LITE cited $5B in laser capacity from just one 2028 fab alone in Greensboro (on higher end ranges). 

And whatever lasers Sivers sell, they're targeting ~50-60+ blended gross margins long term on maybe $3-6 for lower range lasers to $6-$12 for high end custom deployments. But no disclosures around capacity -> revenue conversion yet from Sivers.

Now here's the thing people don't really understand, "why no revenue?" for current opportunities? 

$SIVE pre 2024 focused on custom development for future architectural shifts like CPO. 

For custom deployments:  

- We finally got conversion from 1 of their 4 or so lidar customers this week with ~ $AEVA. 
- ~ $APPL was confirmed ongoing earlier this year with an explanation that "It takes tremendous amount of trials and algorithms way beyond just what we supply to them". 
- All their customers from 2023-2024 like Ayar and 3 others, probably achieve volume in 2028 as CPO takes off. 

Custom high end lasers programs are extremely sticky but take many years and are mainly NRE. And as seen with CPO scale up, faced delays with commercialization over the years.

So $SIVE from the CEO shift in 2024 realized "okay" let's ramp revenue with mass commercialization products today like 70mW/100mW/200mW lasers for 800g/1.6T pluggables. 

And that's where they found $JBL and all your other large pluggable players today during the shortage.

Now...  the work Sivers did in 2023-2024 earlier: Such as $AAPL, Ayar, $AEVA, other lidar/CPO players.

And their new mass commercialization opportunities like $JBL, $GFS, and many pluggables/NPO suppliers in engagement now. 

Have all their inflection points converges 2027 onward, which is why I find the company compelling. 

Where I think management went completely wrong was messaging and near-term execution:

- Deciding to focus on current tiny contracts like Seminex, AllSpace, Tachyon orders felt like the entire focus recently in earnings, shareholder letters, and media commentary

-> Brutal honesty to $SIVE management, majority of Western audiences literally don't care and it's immaterial to the valuation.

$SIVE moved 0% on all of the Seminex/AllSpace/Tachyon order announcements, and even dropped in price. But rallied like 50% on $GFS and something similar on $JBL announcement.

The reason why most took long positions in the first place was CPO.

So if $SIVE wants to go answer questions to Swedish media about "Why are you bleeding out" and defending that with cellular orders explaining pipeline conversion.

That's not going to help people stay long during drawdowns.  

-> Second part was not committing to NASDAQ listing in a certain timeframe and actually executing.

- If there's delays, sure, just say it, but non-committal lawyer-like language is infuriating to hear, especially from the CFO.

I think they'll have that opportunity next month earnings to correct everything.

So wrapping up:

- There's nothing I see remotely close to $SIVE, in terms of % of global CW laser capacity they're coming online with relative to MC. 

- They have a ton commercialization paths, from O-Net, $POET, $JBL, Ayar, $GFS, $AAPL, $AEVA, and many potential hyperscaler/pluggable engagements. 

Even if one or two fall through, the breadth of ongoing quals is so deep + current laser bottleneck is severe, that it's more likely than not many will convert to production. 

It's clear $SIVE wants to focus on dominating the laser chokepoint first, and ended up using their 700m SEK fundraise for capacity expansion. 

But they should focus on communicating the billions in potential economic scale from that laser capacity conversion.

And execute on it.

Drawdowns are the norm. New highs are the exception.

Historically the S&P 500 has spent ~80–95% of its time below a prior peak. Since 1871, 82% of months were underwater (price basis). Since 1950, only about 7% of trading days were at record highs.

Volatility is the price of admission. You cannot earn equity-like long-term returns with bond-like volatility; there is no free lunch. The temporary discomfort of being below your high-water mark is the cost of capturing the upside over decades.

That’s why staying the course matters for investors:

• Markets trend higher over time, but the path is jagged. Recoveries eventually erase most drawdowns. 
• Selling during declines locks in losses and risks missing the rebound. 
• The bigger risk is interrupting compounding by trying to avoid normal volatility.

Being underwater is uncomfortable but expected. The investors who do best treat drawdowns as the entry fee, not a reason to exit. Stay invested and let the long-term maths work.

Historically the S&P 500 has spent ~80–95% of its time below a prior peak. Since 1871, 82% of months were underwater (price basis). Since 1950, only about 7% of trading days were at record highs.

Volatility is the price of admission. You cannot earn equity-like long-term returns with bond-like volatility; there is no free lunch. The temporary discomfort of being below your high-water mark is the cost of capturing the upside over decades.

That’s why staying the course matters for investors:

• Markets trend higher over time, but the path is jagged. Recoveries eventually erase most drawdowns. 
• Selling during declines locks in losses and risks missing the rebound. 
• The bigger risk is interrupting compounding by trying to avoid normal volatility.

Being underwater is uncomfortable but expected. The investors who do best treat drawdowns as the entry fee, not a reason to exit. Stay invested and let the long-term maths work.

Even in the worse cases there are options of soft forks or hard forks before or after the fact. The value as we have seen in the past from other forks and issues is that the community sees the solution in themselves. The stuff about zec or xmr is more people who missed out being opportunistic - there isnt the network value there. Also people are delusional if they think there is a scenario where bitcoin was hacked or something and they thought it could go 0 but their coin could would somehow moon. Government and corporations also know exactly how much is in your bank account, exchange account and any hacker yet we are somehow worried that in some small situation that some people may temporarily link up which address was linked to who. Even for other privacy coins the first trail off an exchange is linked on AML so if governments want to come after you they will just mandate you are taxed at first transfer amount if you cannot prove the chain of transfer. In a scenario of a wallet hack the openness at base layer allows restriction - ie if satoshis coins were hacked you could not allow them to be sold on exchanges for example. Also another reason why you cant just get mass selling. The openness balances rights and responsibilities 

3)I dont think in cycles for investing as im not a trader. Min decade time horizons. As far as crypto space goes only Bitcoin. I imagine you are asking because you want to see if there is anything you are missing so here is the way to think about it in my opinion

Bitcoin is a monetary protocol - so you would need to think about what does it mean for a monetary protocol to succeed or fail 

In the way bitcoin is setup  you would have to think about both the demand and mining side

On the demand side you want to see over long time periods- a deepening and wider interest across different stakeholders

An on mining side long term you want to see hash rate ticking up

In short term both of those can go down so you have to see it on decade time horizons

But since its a monetary protocol and for argument sake more like gold than a stock an invalidation doesnt work the same - like when would you sell all gold and say it failed? its not such a clear line and development and time it takes can be a very long time

With gold for example I see outperformance being driven by china if china and brics moved away from gold I would not want to own it but not because gold would fail and go to 0 but because it would underperform

So its more likely that i would sell bitcoin from it doing so well that i think it would underperform alternatives on decade time horizons than sell because of invalidation

Invalidation on a monetary protocol means its failed which would be 0 value like a currency we no longer use so you have to ask yourself will it go to 0 and if you think it would then you cannot own it in any meaningful sense to begin with. If its not 0 then its probably tremendously valuable

The risk though of underperformance or hedging against self stupidity is important and so you always factor for something going horribly wrong by owning a few assets. 

So with monetary protocols especially given how long they take to really succeed and we only 16-17yrs in it would be difficult to say there was invalidation just based on some thoughts - if you bet on a long term monetary protocol you need to be committed for decades. thats why time horizon matching thesis is so important. You have alot of people trading in and out of a multi decades long thesis and thats not where the upside is

This view is a bit too binary. 

There are many problems that don’t require one to be a user of the system — like consensus or improving snarks. That’s OK since they are core comp sci problems. 

However, the main issue today, is that many problems facing Ethereum are user experience issues caused by the platform itself. 

If the core developers are not using the platform — from an actual usage or building on top of perspective — then they cant properly prioritise the issues that need to be fixed. 

This is why there was so misplaced hype around long term strawman proposals vs fixing low hanging fruit (like sponsored transactions or increasing gas limits) that would immediately help users.

Core Developers, EF, everyone involved needs to treat Ethereum the network as a product and not an ideological-driven machine.
